Multi-port extruded (MPE) aluminum channels are commonly used in air conditioning systems to reduce air-side pressure drop and increase heat transfer coefficients. The channels have flat top and bottom surfaces that contain many microchannel passages to improve the structural stability of the pressurized tube and increase heat transfer rates. An example of a multi-port microchannel tube is shown in Figure 12. Replacing the round tubes in the serpentine design with MPE channels could have many advantages for the TES module because they will create a flat contact surface between the channels and the composite PCM (potentially reducing contact resistance) and allow for the refrigerant and glycol channels to be in direct contact. Figure 12: A flat microchannel extruded tube (source: Tai Xing Group) The proposed microchannel design consists of refrigerant and glycol-water MPEs that are stacked directly on top of each other. The two fluid are routed through the heat exchanger in a single counterflow pass. The total length and width of the MPEs are equal to the length and width of the module, which was set to match the dimensions of the round-tube design (18 inches long and 20.5 inches wide). Each channel pair is sandwiched between two 35-mm thick composite PCM slabs where heat is stored or extracted. The total storage capacity can be scaled by adding glycol-refrigerant tube pairs and the surrounding COMOPSITE PCM, where fluid from the chiller and load is equally distributed to the channels with manifolds. The number of channels in the system were chosen to match the storage capacity of the serpentine design (21.5 kWh or 6.11 ton-h), resulting in about 54 composite PCM slabs. A 2-D transient numerical model was developed to characterize a single unit cell consisting of two fluid channels and two PCM slabs. The model discretizes the system into smaller sub- volumes to track the local temperature and enthalpy changes throughout the discharge process. The model has four types of sub-volumes, or nodes, as shown in Figure 13. The phase change material is discretized in both the x- and y-directions into 400 nodes. The refrigerant, glycol- water, and aluminum walls are discretized into 20 nodes in the x-direction (fluid flow direction). The hot and cold channel aluminum walls are assumed to be isothermal within a node, which 14 This report is available at no cost from the National Renewable Energy Laboratory (NREL) at www.nrel.gov/publications. allows heat to spread throughout the finned structure. The conduction heat transfer rates between PCM nodes is calculated with a discretized version of Fourier’s law, accounting for directional differences in the thermal conductivity of the composite PCM. Heat transfer rates between different types of nodes are calculated by considering all relevant resistances, including fluid convection, contact, and conduction resistances. The enthalpy or temperature changes with time are calculated using an energy balance, shown in the equations in Figure 13.
